screens.title: Containerization with ECS & Fargate
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why containers matter, how Docker packages applications, and how Amazon ECS with Fargate runs those containers without servers. We begin with the core idea: a container bundles application code, runtime, libraries, and settings into a consistent unit that runs the same in dev, test, and production. You will see how a Dockerfile describes that image and how an image becomes multiple running containers. Then we transition to orchestration: ECS manages tasks and services so you can run many containers reliably, and Fargate removes the need to provision EC2 hosts. Throughout, concrete steps show how a simple Node. js app is dockerized, pushed to ECR, and deployed as an ECS service with an Application Load Balancer. Pay attention to the common configuration pitfalls we highlight — like port mappings and C P U/memory sizing — because those are where real deployments typically fail. By the end, you will understand the full developer flow: build an image, push to a registry, define a task, and run it on Fargate. Think about which part you want to try first: writing a Dockerfile or creating the task definition.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Containerization with ECS & Fargate

A practical walkthrough from Dockerfile to a running ECS Fargate service, including ECR and ALB integration.

Estimated lesson time: 15 minutes
Why this chapter matters
Containers give repeatable environments. ECS and Fargate let you operate those containers reliably at scale without server management.
What you'll do
Dockerize a Node.js app, push an image to ECR, create a task definition, and run it as a Fargate service with an Application Load Balancer.
Explore Key Topics
Docker & Images
How Dockerfile produces an image and why images guarantee consistent runs.
ECR Registry
Push and manage container images so ECS can pull them at deploy time.
ECS & Fargate
Run tasks and services without managing EC2 instances when using Fargate.
Visual Concept
Developer
Code + Dockerfile
Build an image locally and push it to a registry so it can be used by ECS.
Cloud
ECR → ECS Fargate
Fargate runs your task definitions; ALB distributes traffic to tasks.
Flow
Dockerfile → Image → ECR → ECS Task Definition → Fargate Service → ALB
Quick start
Start by writing a Dockerfile for your app, build an image locally, test it with docker run, push the image to ECR, and then create a task definition to run the image on Fargate.

screens.title: Docker and Container Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: A container is a self-contained runtime that bundles application code with its runtime, libraries, and configuration so the app runs the same everywhere. The key claim is consistency: developers package everything the application needs and ship that package as an immutable image. A Dockerfile is the human-authored recipe that declares the base runtime, copies application files, installs dependencies, opens ports, and sets the start command. For example, a Node. js app might use a lightweight Node base image, copy package files, run install, copy source, expose port 3000, and set the start command. One concrete example is running the same image locally with docker run and in the cloud via ECS; both use the same binary layers, reducing environment drift. A common misconception is that containers are lightweight VMs; containers share the host kernel and are much lighter. Another pitfall is assuming images include runtime configuration like secrets — they do not; secrets and environment variables must be injected at runtime using task definitions or environment configuration. Takeaway: a Dockerfile produces an image that guarantees consistent execution, but you still must provide runtime configuration and correct ports for networked services. What small step will you try first to verify a new image?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Docker & Containers
Core Concept

What is a container?

A self-contained runtime that includes code, runtime, libraries, and settings. It is built from a Dockerfile into an immutable image.

Concrete example
Run the same Node.js image locally and on ECS; the app behavior should match because the image layers are identical.
Common misconception
Containers are not full VMs. They share the host kernel and are more lightweight; treat configuration and secrets as runtime inputs, not baked into the image.
Key takeaway
Use Dockerfile to create reproducible images and inject environment-specific configuration at runtime.
Analogy
Think of an image as a shipping container: it contains a fixed set of goods and can be loaded on any compatible ship. The runtime configuration is the shipping manifest provided at loading time.
When to use containers
  • When you need consistent dev-to-prod behavior.
  • When scaling stateless services across hosts.
  • When isolating dependencies per service.
Check your understanding
Name one runtime item you should keep out of an image and inject at deploy time. Hint: credentials or secrets.

screens.title: The Dockerfile: From Recipe to Image
screens.narratorSegment: A Dockerfile is the recipe that produces a Docker image. Each instruction has a purpose and contributes to reproducible builds. For the example Node. js Dockerfile you use a lightweight Node base image, set a working directory, copy package metadata, run dependency installation, copy the app code, expose the application port, and declare the command to start the server. This ordering matters: copying package files before installing dependencies lets Docker cache the install layer when source changes do not affect dependencies, saving build time. A concrete example is using the Node 18 alpine image, running npm install, then exposing port 3000 and specifying the start command. A common mistake is copying the entire repository before installing dependencies, which invalidates the cache and slows iterative builds. Another pitfall is forgetting to expose the container port that the app listens on; the image will run, but network traffic from the host or ALB will not reach the application unless port mappings are correct in the task definition. Takeaway: write Dockerfiles with caching and clarity in mind, and always verify the container responds on the expected port.

keyIdea.title: Practical code insight
keyIdea.text: Order Dockerfile steps to maximize cache reuse and ensure the image exposes the correct runtime port for network traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Dockerfile Walkthrough
Definition

Example Dockerfile explained

# Use an official Node.js runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory in the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json to the working directory
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm install

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app runs on
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run the application
CMD [ "npm", "start" ]
Note: Keep dependency install steps separate to leverage layer caching during iterative development.
Why ordering matters
  • Copying package files first allows npm install to be cached.
  • Copying full source after install avoids rebuilding dependencies on every code change.
  • Exposing the port documents the service port; task definitions must map to that port.
Common mistakes
Invalid cache usage, missing EXPOSE, or using heavy base images that slow builds. Test locally with docker run before pushing.
Key Takeaway

Structure Dockerfile for cache-friendly builds and match exposed ports to your runtime configuration.

screens.title: Build, Tag, and Push: Local to ECR Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: The developer workflow moves an image from your workstation into a managed registry so ECS can pull it at runtime. The essential steps are build, tag, authenticate to ECR, and push. For example, build locally with the docker build command and tag it for your ECR repository name. Authenticate the Docker CLI to ECR using the provider's CLI to get a short-lived password and pipe it into docker login. Then push the tagged image to the repository. A concrete example in the lesson shows tagging an image with the full ECR repository URI and pushing it. Why this matters: storing images in ECR centralizes versioned artifacts, allows ECS to fetch consistent images, and integrates with CI/CD pipelines to automate deployments on commits. A common mistake is failing to tag the image using the correct account and region in the repository URI, which results in a push error. Another pitfall is relying on cached local images without confirming the push succeeded. Takeaway: automate these steps in CI so builds are reproducible and pushes are reliable. Build, Tag, and Push: Local to ECR Workflow means build, correctly tag with your ecr uri, authenticate, and push to make your image available to ecs and ci/cd pipelines.. In practical terms, commands and steps to get an image from your machine into amazon ecr. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Build & Push
Process Flow

Local build to ECR push

Step-by-step commands
# Build image locally
docker build -t my-web-app .

# Tag for ECR (replace placeholders)
docker tag my-web-app:latest 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest

# Authenticate to ECR (example AWS CLI)
aws ecr get-login-password --region YOUR_REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.YOUR_REGION.amazonaws.com

# Push the image
docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest
Automate these in CI to build and push on each commit.
Common errors
  • Wrong ECR URI or region in the tag causes push failures.
  • Expired login token for ECR; re-authenticate before push.
  • Pushing large images without optimizing layers slows CI pipelines.
Check
Confirm the image appears in the ECR console and the digest matches the local build before proceeding to create a task definition.

screens.title: ECS Components: Cluster, Task Definition, Task, Service
screens.narratorSegment: ECS organizes container workloads using a few simple concepts. A cluster is a logical grouping of tasks and services; it can contain Fargate tasks, EC2-backed tasks, or both depending on your launch choice. A task definition is the blueprint: it names the container image, assigns C P U and memory, maps ports, and declares environment variables and the execution role. When you run a task, the task definition is instantiated and becomes a running task — a process performing the work. A service ensures a desired number of task copies run and provides health checks, replacement of unhealthy tasks, and integration with load balancers. For example, creating a service with desired count 2 and an Application Load Balancer allows the ALB to route traffic across the two task instances. A misconception is treating clusters as servers; clusters are logical and, with Fargate, you do not manage their hosts. The practical significance: design your task definition to include the right C P U and memory to avoid OOM or throttling, and use services to maintain availability. Consider what metrics you'll monitor — task health and C P U utilization — and configure auto scaling when appropriate.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › ECS Components
Architecture

Cluster → Task Definition → Task → Service

Cluster
Logical grouping of tasks and services. With Fargate you don't manage the host instances.
Task Definition
Blueprint declaring image, CPU, memory, port mappings, and environment. The task role and execution role manage permissions.
Task
A running instantiation of a task definition. Multiple tasks can run from the same definition.
Service
Maintains a desired count of tasks, replaces unhealthy tasks, and integrates with load balancers and auto scaling policies.
Design guidance

Select CPU and memory in the task definition to match your workload; oversizing wastes cost, undersizing causes failures. Use services for availability and ALB integration for traffic distribution.

screens.title: EC2 Launch Type vs Fargate
screens.narratorSegment: ECS supports two primary launch types: EC2 and AWS Fargate. The EC2 launch type means you provision and manage EC2 instances that act as the host pool for containers. You control instance types, AMIs, and cluster scaling, which gives flexibility for specialized host-level configuration but also increases operational overhead: patching, scaling, and capacity management fall on you. By contrast, Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. You specify C P U and memory per task and Fargate runs them without provisioning EC2 hosts. For most new applications, Fargate reduces operational burden and is recommended because it simplifies scaling and operations. A concrete scenario: if you need a custom kernel module or GPUs tightly coupled to host hardware, EC2 may be appropriate. A common misconception is that Fargate is always more expensive; cost depends on utilization patterns and control needs. The practical takeaway: choose Fargate when you prefer to focus on code and reduce infrastructure management, and reserve EC2 when you need host-level control or specialized hardware. EC2 Launch Type vs Fargate means fargate offloads host management; ec2 gives host-level control. choose based on operational needs and hardware requirements.. In practical terms, when to manage ec2 instances and when to choose serverless containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Fargate vs EC2
Comparison

EC2 Launch Type vs Fargate

EC2 Launch Type
  • You manage the EC2 instances and AMIs.
  • Good for custom host configs, drivers, or GPUs.
  • Requires patching, scaling, and capacity planning.
AWS Fargate
  • Serverless containers: no EC2 provisioning.
  • Specify CPU and memory per task; platform manages the rest.
  • Recommended for most new applications to reduce ops burden.
Decision guidance
If you need host-level control, choose EC2. If you prefer to focus on code and reduce infrastructure maintenance, choose Fargate. Consider cost and utilization patterns when making a selection.

screens.title: Create a Task Definition and Service
screens.narratorSegment: A task definition is the formal blueprint ECS uses to run containers. When creating one, specify the container name, the image URI from ECR, and required C P U and memory. Port mappings tell ECS which container port will receive traffic; this must match the port your application listens on. You must also choose the networking mode; for Fargate use awsvpc so each task gets an elastic network interface and security group settings. Assign the ecsTaskExecutionRole to allow pulling images and writing logs. After the task definition is in place, create a service that references it, choose Fargate as the launch type, and set the desired task count. Optionally attach an Application Load Balancer and configure a target group to forward traffic to the container port. A common misconfiguration is mismatched port numbers between the task definition and the ALB target group. Another is insufficient C P U or memory, which causes tasks to fail to start. The practical check is: after creating the service, ensure tasks reach RUNNING state and health checks from the ALB pass. If not, review logs and security group rules. What monitoring will you place to detect under-provisioning?

keyIdea.text: Task definitions specify runtime details; services run and maintain tasks and connect them to load balancers and scaling policies.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Task Definition & Service
Process Flow

Define and run your container

Essential task definition fields
  • Container image URI pointing to ECR.
  • CPU and memory allocation per task.
  • Port mappings: container port → host/target group port.
  • Task role and execution role for permissions.
Creating the service
Choose Fargate launch type, set desired count, configure VPC and subnets, attach a security group, and optionally create an Application Load Balancer with a target group pointing to the container port.
Validation checklist
  • Task status transitions to RUNNING.
  • ALB target group shows healthy targets after health checks.
  • Logs show application listening on the expected port.
  • Security groups allow ALB to reach the task ENI on the mapped port.

screens.title: Load Balancer Integration and Auto Scaling
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating an Application Load Balancer with an ECS service provides stable, discoverable endpoints and distributes traffic across tasks. When creating the service, choose to attach an ALB and create a target group that forwards traffic to the container port your task listens on. Health checks from the ALB determine whether a task receives traffic; set health check paths and intervals appropriate for your application. For scalability, configure service auto scaling using target tracking policies such as C P U utilization. For example, set a target of 70 percent C P U to increase task count when load rises. The practical significance is resilience: if a task fails, the service replaces it and the ALB stops routing to the unhealthy target. Common misconfigurations include misaligned health checks or target group ports that do not match container ports, resulting in never-healthy targets. screens.title: Pitfalls: Port Mappings, Resources, and IAM Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Deployments often fail for a few repeated reasons. First, incorrect port mappings: if your container listens on port 8080 but the task definition or ALB target group points to 80, the ALB cannot reach the application. Always confirm the container port in the task definition matches the port your app exposes. Second, insufficient C P U or memory: under-provisioned tasks may fail to start or run slowly. Choose a task size aligned with expected workload and monitor C P U and memory metrics to adjust. Third, missing or incorrect IAM roles: the ecsTaskExecutionRole must exist with policies to pull from ECR and publish logs. Without it, Fargate cannot pull images or create CloudWatch logs. Finally, networking and security groups: the ALB needs permission to reach the task ENI on the mapped port. A concrete troubleshooting step is to check task logs for application errors, review the ALB target health, and verify security group rules. Misconception: logs are always immediately available — sometimes tasks fail during startup before logs initialize. Takeaway: follow a checklist: verify image in ECR, check task definition ports and resources, confirm IAM roles, and validate security group connectivity.

Example project files

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why containers matter, how Docker packages applications, and how Amazon ECS with Fargate runs those containers without servers. We begin with the core idea: a container bundles application code, runtime, libraries, and settings into a consistent unit that runs the same in dev, test, and production. You will see how a Dockerfile describes that image and how an image becomes multiple running containers. Then we transition to orchestration: ECS manages tasks and services so you can run many containers reliably, and Fargate removes the need to provision EC2 hosts. Throughout, concrete steps show how a simple Node. js app is dockerized, pushed to ECR, and deployed as an ECS service with an Application Load Balancer. Pay attention to the common configuration pitfalls we highlight — like port mappings and C P U/memory sizing — because those are where real deployments typically fail. By the end, you will understand the full developer flow: build an image, push to a registry, define a task, and run it on Fargate. Think about which part you want to try first: writing a Dockerfile or creating the task definition.

These objectives focus on developer skills you can apply immediately. First, you will explain Docker and containerization: what a container packages and why that packaging solves environment inconsistency. An example objective is describing a Dockerfile and how an image is created. Second, you will describe ECS components and the difference between Fargate and EC2 launch types. You should be able to explain when to manage EC2 instances yourself and when Fargate is a better choice. Third, you will define an ECS task definition and create a service that keeps your containers running. This includes setting C P U and memory, port mappings, and the execution role. Lastly, you will implement a developer workflow: write a Dockerfile, build an image, push to ECR, create a task definition, and deploy a Fargate service. Each objective pairs a clear outcome with a practical reason: consistency, operational simplicity, reliable runtime, and repeatable deployment. Practice each step until you can perform the flow with confidence and notice where misconfigurations commonly occur.

These four practical objectives reinforce applied skills. For Docker, you will write a Dockerfile that installs dependencies and starts the app so you can build and run images locally. For ECS components, you will map the mental model: cluster groups tasks, a task definition is the blueprint, a task is a running instance, and a service ensures the desired count. For task and service creation, you will specify C P U and memory and set port mappings and the task execution role; practice prevents common misconfigurations like wrong ports or missing permissions. For deployment workflow, you will push an image to ECR and create an ECS service attached to an Application Load Balancer and optional auto scaling. Each objective includes why it matters: repeatability, reliability, security, and operational simplicity. As you practice, verify the app through the ALB DNS and check task logs for errors. Ask yourself after each run: did the task start, did the ALB route traffic, and are there permission errors? These checks will build confidence.

A container is a self-contained runtime that bundles application code with its runtime, libraries, and configuration so the app runs the same everywhere. The key claim is consistency: developers package everything the application needs and ship that package as an immutable image. A Dockerfile is the human-authored recipe that declares the base runtime, copies application files, installs dependencies, opens ports, and sets the start command. For example, a Node. js app might use a lightweight Node base image, copy package files, run install, copy source, expose port 3000, and set the start command. One concrete example is running the same image locally with docker run and in the cloud via ECS; both use the same binary layers, reducing environment drift. A common misconception is that containers are lightweight VMs; containers share the host kernel and are much lighter. Another pitfall is assuming images include runtime configuration like secrets — they do not; secrets and environment variables must be injected at runtime using task definitions or environment configuration. Takeaway: a Dockerfile produces an image that guarantees consistent execution, but you still must provide runtime configuration and correct ports for networked services. What small step will you try first to verify a new image?

A Dockerfile is the recipe that produces a Docker image. Each instruction has a purpose and contributes to reproducible builds. For the example Node. js Dockerfile you use a lightweight Node base image, set a working directory, copy package metadata, run dependency installation, copy the app code, expose the application port, and declare the command to start the server. This ordering matters: copying package files before installing dependencies lets Docker cache the install layer when source changes do not affect dependencies, saving build time. A concrete example is using the Node 18 alpine image, running npm install, then exposing port 3000 and specifying the start command. A common mistake is copying the entire repository before installing dependencies, which invalidates the cache and slows iterative builds. Another pitfall is forgetting to expose the container port that the app listens on; the image will run, but network traffic from the host or ALB will not reach the application unless port mappings are correct in the task definition. Takeaway: write Dockerfiles with caching and clarity in mind, and always verify the container responds on the expected port.

The developer workflow moves an image from your workstation into a managed registry so ECS can pull it at runtime. The essential steps are build, tag, authenticate to ECR, and push. For example, build locally with the docker build command and tag it for your ECR repository name. Authenticate the Docker CLI to ECR using the provider's CLI to get a short-lived password and pipe it into docker login. Then push the tagged image to the repository. A concrete example in the lesson shows tagging an image with the full ECR repository URI and pushing it. Why this matters: storing images in ECR centralizes versioned artifacts, allows ECS to fetch consistent images, and integrates with CI/CD pipelines to automate deployments on commits. A common mistake is failing to tag the image using the correct account and region in the repository URI, which results in a push error. Another pitfall is relying on cached local images without confirming the push succeeded. Takeaway: automate these steps in CI so builds are reproducible and pushes are reliable. Build, Tag, and Push: Local to ECR Workflow means build, correctly tag with your ecr uri, authenticate, and push to make your image available to ecs and ci/cd pipelines.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ECS organizes container workloads using a few simple concepts. A cluster is a logical grouping of tasks and services; it can contain Fargate tasks, EC2-backed tasks, or both depending on your launch choice. A task definition is the blueprint: it names the container image, assigns C P U and memory, maps ports, and declares environment variables and the execution role. When you run a task, the task definition is instantiated and becomes a running task — a process performing the work. A service ensures a desired number of task copies run and provides health checks, replacement of unhealthy tasks, and integration with load balancers. For example, creating a service with desired count 2 and an Application Load Balancer allows the ALB to route traffic across the two task instances. A misconception is treating clusters as servers; clusters are logical and, with Fargate, you do not manage their hosts. The practical significance: design your task definition to include the right C P U and memory to avoid OOM or throttling, and use services to maintain availability. Consider what metrics you'll monitor — task health and C P U utilization — and configure auto scaling when appropriate.

ECS supports two primary launch types: EC2 and AWS Fargate. The EC2 launch type means you provision and manage EC2 instances that act as the host pool for containers. You control instance types, AMIs, and cluster scaling, which gives flexibility for specialized host-level configuration but also increases operational overhead: patching, scaling, and capacity management fall on you. By contrast, Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. You specify C P U and memory per task and Fargate runs them without provisioning EC2 hosts. For most new applications, Fargate reduces operational burden and is recommended because it simplifies scaling and operations. A concrete scenario: if you need a custom kernel module or GPUs tightly coupled to host hardware, EC2 may be appropriate. A common misconception is that Fargate is always more expensive; cost depends on utilization patterns and control needs. The practical takeaway: choose Fargate when you prefer to focus on code and reduce infrastructure management, and reserve EC2 when you need host-level control or specialized hardware.
